title: MVCC and isolation levels
problem: Two transactions each check a rule, each write a different row, and both commit, leaving the database in a state neither of them would have allowed.
summary: MVCC keeps several versions of a row so readers never block writers, and each transaction reads a snapshot. Snapshot isolation still permits write skew, which serializable snapshot isolation or explicit locks prevent, and old versions must be vacuumed or purged.
catTip: Two humans each check the bowl, each see food, each decide the other will refill it. That is snapshot isolation in my own kitchen. Serializable would make one of them wait or retry, and I would eat.

recall.q: Two on-call doctors each check that at least two are rostered, then each remove themselves; both commit and nobody is on call. Name the anomaly and two ways to prevent it.
recall.a: Write skew: disjoint writes after reading overlapping data, which snapshot isolation allows. Prevent it with SERIALIZABLE (serializable snapshot isolation, retrying on SQLSTATE 40001) or by locking the rows the decision depends on with SELECT FOR UPDATE.

guide.breaks: Without MVCC every reader waits for every writer on the same rows; with MVCC but without understanding write skew, check-then-act rules that span rows silently break under Repeatable Read.
guide.tradeoffs: Old versions consume space and must be vacuumed or purged, long transactions block that cleanup, and SERIALIZABLE buys correctness with aborts the application has to retry.
guide.explainSimply: The database keeps old copies of a row so that someone reading it never waits for someone changing it; each transaction reads a frozen snapshot, like that morning's newspaper edition. The catch is two people reading the same edition and each making a decision the other did not see. Serializable mode notices that and makes one of them redo their work.
guide.hint: Think about two transactions that read the same rows but write different ones, and about what happens to the rows nobody can see any more.

meow: New version, old version, snapshot decides who sees what. Write skew sneaks past; serializable says retry, meow.

quiz.prompt: Under PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read, which anomaly can still occur?
quiz.explanation: PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is snapshot isolation and blocks dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads, so write skew (disjoint writes after overlapping reads) is what remains and needs Serializable. Phantoms are permitted by the SQL standard's definition but not by PostgreSQL's implementation.

quiz.prompt: A nightly report runs one six-hour transaction on the primary. Users notice the orders table keeps growing and scans slow down even though rows are deleted daily. What is the mechanism?
options: The report holds row locks that block the deletes
The report's snapshot pins old row versions, so VACUUM cannot remove dead tuples created since it began
Transaction ID wraparound has already happened
quiz.explanation: MVCC keeps every version younger than the oldest snapshot, so the long transaction blocks cleanup rather than the deletes. Autovacuum is on by default, and wraparound would stop the server rather than merely slow scans.

cards.q: Explain what xmin and xmax on a PostgreSQL row version mean and how an UPDATE changes them.
cards.a: xmin is the ID of the transaction that created the version and xmax the ID of the one that deleted or replaced it (zero while live). An UPDATE writes a new version with xmin set to the updater and stamps the old version's xmax with the same ID; visibility is then decided against a snapshot plus the commit status in pg_xact.

cards.q: A booking service must sell each seat once. Compare a unique index, SELECT FOR UPDATE and SERIALIZABLE for enforcing it.
cards.a: A unique index on show and seat is cheapest and strongest: the second insert fails at any isolation level. SELECT FOR UPDATE serialises check-then-insert by locking rows that already exist, which does not cover a row not yet inserted. SERIALIZABLE detects the conflict and aborts one transaction, which must retry.

glossary.note: Keeping several versions of each row so readers see a snapshot while writers create new versions.
PostgreSQL's serializable mode: snapshot reads plus detection of dangerous read-write dependency patterns, aborting one transaction instead of blocking.
PostgreSQL's 32-bit transaction identifier, stamped on row versions as xmin and xmax.
